extracted.intended_audience: manufacturers, printers, engineers, and students of industrial/printing techniques
extracted.subtask_description: Describes principles, methods, and quality/production considerations for copying and printing processes (copperplate, surface printing, lithography, casting, moulding, etc.), with examples and practical guidance on durability, accuracy, and throughput.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set-off sheet / blanket maintenance and ink transfer
rubrics_metrics.description: When work printed is laid, it is guarded from soiling by a sheet of paper called the set-off sheet... In the new method of printing by machinery, no set-off sheet is used, but a blanket is employed as its substitute; this does not require changing above once in five thousand impressions, and instances have occurred of its remaining sufficiently clean for twenty thousand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of a blanket greatly reduces ink transfer per impression; frequency of changing the set-off sheet/blanket is an indicator of the amount of superfluous ink (old method: change ~every 100 impressions; best old method once in 12; machine blankets: once in 2000–5000, sometimes 20000). This gives empirical evidence of cleanliness and economy of machine printing versus hand methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity of pieces produced by the same tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing is more remarkable... than the perfect identity of things manufactured by the same tool. If the top of a circular box is to be made to fit over the lower part... After adjustment, if a thousand boxes are made, no additional care is required; the tool is always carried up to the stop, and each box will be equally adapted to every lid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate production by the repeatability/interchangeability of parts produced from the same tool or machine stop; a properly adjusted tool should produce identical items without further trial for large batches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy of machinery (vs manual)
rubrics_metrics.description: The accuracy with which machinery executes its work is, perhaps, one of its most important advantages: it may, however, be contended, that a considerable portion of this advantage may be resolved into saving of time; for it generally happens, that any improvement in tools increases the quantity of work done in a given time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether improved accuracy arises from inherent machine precision or from increased throughput enabling careful setup; consider time savings and reduced variability as components of 'accuracy' advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superiority of turning for precision
rubrics_metrics.description: Of all the operations of mechanical art, that of turning is the most perfect... there exists a tendency in them both to become portions of spheres... It is more easy to make a good circle than to produce a straight line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing/evaluating turned parts, expect excellent circular symmetry; anticipate greater difficulty achieving perfect flat/straight surfaces. Use lathe/turning where circular precision is paramount.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of copying and amortized care on originals
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle alluded to is that of copying, taken in its most extensive sense. Almost unlimited pains are, in some instances, bestowed on the original, from which a series of copies is to be produced; the larger the number of these copies, the more care and pains can the manufacturer afford to lavish upon the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide investment in original tooling/patterns based on expected production volume; high up-front cost/effort is justified when amortized over many copies (tool may cost thousands times a single specimen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of copying methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Operations of copying are effected under the following circumstances: By printing from cavities; By stamping; By printing from surface; By punching; By casting; With elongation; By moulding; With altered dimensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this classification to choose the appropriate copying technique depending on material, desired fidelity, dimensional alteration, and production scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copper-plate printing (printing from cavities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Copies are made by transferring to paper, by means of pressure, a thick ink, from the hollows and lines cut in the copper. An artist will sometimes exhaust the labour of one or two years upon engraving a plate, which will not, in some cases, furnish above five hundred copies in a state of perfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copper-plate engraving yields high-fidelity impressions but limited perfect impressions (often ~500) for highly worked plates; plan for plate deterioration and limited-run expectations when selecting copper tooling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engraving on steel (durability of plates)
rubrics_metrics.description: This is an art in most respects similar to engraving on copper, except that the number of copies is far less limited. A bank-note engraved as a copper-plate, will not give above three thousand impressions without a sensible deterioration... two impressions (one early, one after 70–80k) were difficult to distinguish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steel engraving yields far greater durability (tens of thousands of impressions) and is suitable for extremely high-run items (e.g., bank-notes) where plate longevity and near-identity over many impressions is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music-printing (materials effect on appearance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Music is usually printed from pewter plates... The metal being much softer than copper, is liable to scratches, which detain a small portion of the ink. This is the reason of the dirty appearance of printed music.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material choice for plates affects surface quality and susceptibility to scratches; softer metals hold ink in scratches and yield dirty appearance—consider alternative methods (surface-printing) to improve sharpness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calico printing from cylinders (high throughput and scraper control)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many patterns on printed calicos are copies by printing from copper cylinders... One portion of the cylinders is exposed to the ink, whilst an elastic scraper of stuffed leather, by being pressed forcibly against another part, removes all superfluous ink from the surface previously to its reaching the cloth. A piece of calico twenty-eight yards in length rolls through this press and is printed in four or five minutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cylinder engraving + scraper allows very high-speed, continuous printing; control of scraper and ink exposure is critical to quality and consistency over long runs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stencilling / printing from perforated sheets (economy vs fidelity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Very thin brass is sometimes perforated in the form of letters... This method, which affords rather a coarse copy, is sometimes used for paper with which rooms are covered, and more especially for the borders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stencilling is economical and suitable for matching or coarse patterns where high fidelity is not required; use for low-cost reproduction or patching old patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discharge printing on dyed cloth (reverse operation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The reverse operation — that of discharging a part of the colour from a cloth already dyed — is performed. A number of handkerchiefs are pressed... a fluid which has the property of discharging the red dye is poured upon that plate... the pattern of each is a copy of the perforated metal-plate used in the process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For dyed fabrics, consider discharge-printing to produce patterns by removing dye rather than adding pigment; requires precise pressure and application to avoid spread beyond pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printing from wooden blocks (surface printing principles)
rubrics_metrics.description: A block of box-wood is the substance out of which the pattern is formed... the workman cuts away with sharp tools every part except the lines to be represented in the impression. The ink... is spread upon the surface which remains, and is thence transferred to the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wood-block printing is a surface-printing technique appropriate for bold designs; it is the reverse of cavity engraving and requires uniform surface relief for even inking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printing from movable types (modularity and reuse)
rubrics_metrics.description: This is the most important in its influence, of all the arts of copying. It possesses a singular peculiarity, in the immense subdivision of the parts that form the pattern. After that pattern has furnished thousands of copies, the same individual elements may be arranged again and again in other forms...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Movable type enables combinatorial reuse of elements to produce myriad originals with low marginal cost per new arrangement; ideal for text-heavy, variable-content mass production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereotype printing (fixed-patter, large runs, and accuracy)
rubrics_metrics.description: This mode of producing copies is very similar to the preceding: but as the original pattern is incapable of change, it is only applied to cases where an extraordinary number of copies are demanded, or where the work consists of figures, and it is of great importance to ensure accuracy. Alterations may be made in it from time to time; and thus mathematical tables may, by the gradual extirpation of error, at last become perfect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use stereotype for extremely large, unchanging runs or when high accuracy is required (e.g., tables). While fixed, it allows iterative correction over editions and integration with wood-cuts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calico printing from blocks (multicolor registration and block sets)
rubrics_metrics.description: This is a mode of copying, by surface-printing, from the ends of small pieces of copper wire... If the block be placed upon... cloth... By the former method only one colour could be used; but by this plan, after the flower of a rose... has been printed with one set of blocks, the leaves may be printed of another colour by a different set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multi-color surface printing requires separate block sets for each color and precise registration; planning and multiple sets increase cost but allow multicolor patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oil-cloth printing (color set dependency on cost)
rubrics_metrics.description: After the canvass... has been covered with paint of one uniform tint, the remainder of the processes... are a series of copyings by surface-printing, from patterns formed upon wooden blocks. Each colour requires a distinct set of blocks, and thus those oil-cloths with the greatest variety of colours are most expensive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cost scales with number of colors because each color needs distinct tooling; balance aesthetic needs vs production cost when designing multicolor oil-cloth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letter-copying methods and repeat limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: A sheet of very thin paper is damped, and placed upon the writing to be copied... The two papers are then passed through a rolling press, and a portion of the ink from one paper is transferred to the other... Both these arts are very limited in their extent, two or three being the utmost number of repetitions they allow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Letter-copying by damp transfer or carbon-like lamp-black methods yields limited repeats (typically 2–3); plan accordingly for low-repetition duplication needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printing on china (transfer via flexible intermediary)
rubrics_metrics.description: As the surfaces to which the impression is to be conveyed are often curved... the ink or paint is first transferred from the copper to some flexible substance, such as paper, or an elastic compound of glue and treacle. It is almost immediately conveyed from this to the unbaked biscuit, to which it more readily adheres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For curved/irregular surfaces, use a flexible transfer medium to move the design from plate to object; timing and adhesion to the unbaked substrate are critical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lithographic printing (water/grease chemical principle and reprinting use-case)
rubrics_metrics.description: The original is a drawing made on a stone of a slightly porous nature; the ink employed for tracing it is made of such greasy materials that when water is poured over the stone it shall not wet the lines... One application is the reprinting of works which have just arrived from other countries... By similar means the other side of the newspaper may be copied on another stone...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lithography depends on chemical affinity differences; it is suitable for rapid reprinting (e.g., newspapers) and facsimiles, but transferability from old printed ink to stone depends on ink chemistry and age, possibly requiring sacrifice of copies or chemical restoration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Register-printing (double-sided exact superposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Register-printing... is to make it appear as if the ink had penetrated through the paper... The block which gives the impression is always accurately brought down to the same place by means of a hinge... The perfection of this mode of printing depends in a great measure on finding some soft substance like leather... Impressions thus obtained are usually fainter on the lower side; and... rather more ink is put on the block at the first than at the second impression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Achieve precise double-sided alignment by hinged block and intermediate soft surface (leather); compensate for fainter under-side impressions by adjusting ink amounts and selecting suitable intermediate materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Casting (patterns, moulds, shrinkage compensation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The art of casting, by pouring substances in a fluid state into a mould which retains them until they become solid, is essentially an art of copying... As the metals shrink in cooling, the pattern is made larger than the intended copy; and in extricating it from the sand... some little difference will occur in the size of the cavity which it leaves. In smaller works... a mould of metal is employed which has been formed with considerable care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design patterns and moulds accounting for shrinkage and extraction variability; use metal moulds for high-accuracy castings and include provisions (e.g., jets) to supply deficiency during cooling (bullets).

rubrics_metrics.name: Casting in plaster (moulding delicate originals)
rubrics_metrics.description: This is a mode of copying applied... to produce accurate representations of the human form, of statues, or of rare fossils... The property [of plaster] of remaining for a short time in a state of fluidity renders it admirably adapted... adhesion... is effectually prevented by oiling the surface on which it is poured. The mould formed round the subject... removed in separate pieces and then reunited, is that in which the copy is cast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use plaster for detailed moulds of delicate originals; prevent adhesion by oiling and construct moulds in separable pieces for removal and reassembly to cast accurate reproductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Casting in wax (appearance vs copy volume)
rubrics_metrics.description: This mode of copying, aided by proper colouring, offers the most successful imitations of many objects of natural history... The art of copying in wax does not usually afford the multitude of copies which flow from many similar operations. This number is checked by the subsequent stages... form alone is given by casting; the colouring must be the work of the pencil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wax casting yields highly realistic single items but low throughput due to hand-colouring; suitable for display models where realism is more important than quantity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moulding (plastic materials for mass uniformity)
rubrics_metrics.description: This method of producing multitudes of individuals having an exact resemblance in external shape is adopted very widely in the arts. The substances employed are... in a soft or plastic state; they are then compressed by mechanical force, sometimes assisted by heat, into a mould of the required form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moulding is the preferred method for high-volume, uniform external shapes (bricks, tiles, embossed china, horn, etc.); material preparation and mould care determine surface quality and production rate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bricks & tiles (moulding process and production rates)
rubrics_metrics.description: An oblong box of wood... is the mould from which every brick is formed... A very skilful moulder has occasionally, in a long summer's day, delivered from ten to eleven thousand bricks; but a fair average day's work is from five to six thousand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess labor expectations and throughput for moulded building materials; production rates depend on worker skill and process efficiency—plan workforce and drying space accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embossed china and partial moulding/lathe union
rubrics_metrics.description: Many forms given to earthenware... are not capable of being executed in the lathe of the potter. The embossed ornaments... become easy and uniform when made by pressing the soft material... In many works, one part only of the article is moulded... whilst the under side is figured by the lathe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine moulding and lathe-turning to balance complex ornamentation and turned surfaces; invest in quality moulds for high repeatability of decorative elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Glass seals & imitation by moulding (heating and mould finish)
rubrics_metrics.description: A small cylindrical rod of coloured glass is heated... The operator then pinches it between the ends of a pair of nippers, which are formed of brass, and on one side of which has been carved in relief the device intended for the seal... When care has been taken in heating the glass properly, and when the mould has been well finished, the seals thus produced are not bad imitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control heating and mould finishing closely when producing glass imitations; small tooling imperfections or insufficient heating reduce fidelity—yet mass-produced imitations can be very cheap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Square glass bottles (moulded marking and volume consistency)
rubrics_metrics.description: A mould of iron, or of copper, is provided of the intended size, on the inside of which are engraved the names required... The mould is now closed, and by blowing strongly into the bottle the glass is forced against its sides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To achieve consistent volume and permanent maker markings, use two-part heated moulds with internal engraving; blowing pressure must be controlled to fill cavity and preserve legibility of engravings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moulded wooden snuff-boxes, horn handles, and tortoiseshell (softening and pressing)
rubrics_metrics.description: The wood, or horn, out of which they are formed, is softened by long boiling in water, and whilst in this state it is forced into moulds of iron, or steel... Horn possesses the property of becoming soft by the action of water and of heat, fits it for many useful purposes. It is pressed into moulds, and becomes embossed with figures in relief... Moulding tortoise-shell is more rarely employed due to superior raw material price.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For thermally/chemically softened organic materials, use heat/water softening followed by pressing into moulds for embossed/curved parts; material costs may limit applicability (e.g., tortoiseshell).
